pr_title: Rework split, layout, workspace_layout, and move commands to work like i3
pr_body:
EDIT: Hijacking top comment b/c this PR is barely related to what it started as anyway

Hey you. Lurker. Please test.

---
Fix #5755 

This is intended to match i3's behavior here:

https://github.com/i3/i3/blob/3cd1c45eba6de073bc4300eebb4e1cc1a0c4479a/src/tree.c#L354

However, this isn't quite right (I know you haven't marked it as ready for review yet etc., but anyway). The check for the parent layout to be a [vh]split is actually necessary, because if you have a `T[app1]` and vsplit, this *should* result in `T[V[app1]]`, _not_ `V[app1]`.

Probably a good idea to leave a comment linking to the i3 source here, because this is pretty non-obvious.

Fixes #5755, #5754, Re-fixes #5157,  #4038.

This only differs in i3 in that i3 always has the wrapping `H` for the workspace, whereas Sway often changes the workspace layout itself.

i3 doesn't always wrap workspaces, just when changinging the layout on a single container. Otherwise they change the workspace layout. The difference here is in the behavior of the layout command, which I guess I should also update to match:

https://github.com/i3/i3/blob/3cd1c45eba6de073bc4300eebb4e1cc1a0c4479a/src/con.c#L1817

The sway(5) man page will probably need to be updated with a proper description of `workspace_layout` too.

Yeah, it's tricky. Bit of a meta-comment, and you may already have a testing setup that works for you, but I've found the following to be very helpful in comparing i3 with Sway:

* [script to dump layout](https://github.com/swaywm/sway/issues/5157#issuecomment-614311103), works on both i3 and Sway
```
$ cat ~/gettree.sh                                                                                                                                    
swaymsg -t get_tree|jq "def f: {name, type, layout, nodes: [.nodes[]|f]}; recurse(.nodes[])|select(.name == \"$1\")|f"
$ ~/gettree.sh 1   # get tree of workspace 1
```

* start Xephyr

```
$ Xephyr +iglx -br -ac -resizeable -noreset -keybd ephyr,,xkbmodel=evdev :2 &
```

* start i3 within Xephyr

```
$ unset XDG_RUNTIME_DIR && unset WAYLAND_DISPLAY && DISPLAY=:2 i3
```

* passthrough mode in Sway config so you can use conflicting keybinds within Xephyr i3

```
mode "passthrough" {
	bindsym $mod+p mode default
}

bindsym $mod+p mode passthrough
```

So here's an interesting layout with `workspace_layout tabbed`:

`begin` -> `H[T[app app*]]`
`move right` -> `H[T[app] T[app*]]` (matches i3)
`move up` -> `V[T[app*] H[T[app]]]` (matches i3, your scenario above)

In the last move, though it's pretty unwieldy, the sway layout is the one that matches my mental model of the i3 tree. I'd guess it's special cased somewhere, but atm I'm not sure what i3 is doing here to get the simpler layout.

I'd guess it's this:

https://github.com/i3/i3/blob/1f0c628cde40cf87371481041b7197344e0417c6/src/tree.c#L638-L651

```c
/*
 * tree_flatten() removes pairs of redundant split containers, e.g.:
 *       [workspace, horizontal]
 *   [v-split]           [child3]
 *   [h-split]
 * [child1] [child2]
 * In this example, the v-split and h-split container are redundant.
 * Such a situation can be created by moving containers in a direction which is
 * not the orientation of their parent container. i3 needs to create a new
 * split container then and if you move containers this way multiple times,
 * redundant chains of split-containers can be the result.
 *
 */
void tree_flatten(Con *con) {
```

Called right at the end of `tree_move` on `croot`, which looks like, well, the root of the workspace: https://github.com/i3/i3/blob/1f0c628cde40cf87371481041b7197344e0417c6/src/move.c#L388

We don't have a version of this in Sway AFAICT; `container_flatten` moves up the tree rather than down it.

issue_context.title: Workspace switching order is different from i3's when using multiple outputs
issue_context.body:
In i3, there are commands `workspace prev`, and `workspace next`, which switch to next or previous workspaces. Sway has the same commands too, but the order in which they switch between workspaces is inconsistent with i3's.

Imagine a situation: workspaces 1, 2 and 4 are on first output, and workspace 3 is on the second, and workspace 1 is the one currently focused.

In i3, repeatedly pressing a binding for command `workspace next` would switch from workspace 1 to workspace 2, and then 3 (moving focus to the other output since that's where the workspace is), and then 4 (switching focus back to first output) - consistent with the order of workspaces.

In Sway, repeatedly pressing such a binding would switch from workspace 1, to workspace 2, and then jump over and switch to workspace 4, and after that will go back and switch to workspace 3 on the different output.

I haven't found a command in Sway to switch between workspaces based on their true order, no matter in which order are the outputs on which these workspaces are, instead of switching based on the order of workspaces on the current output and order of outputs.

review_comments: Somewhat an aside from the meat of this PR, but I think we should have something like a `container_reset_geometry` for this since these lines appear in a lot of other places.
You're probably right, but I think I'll hold off adding that in this PR.
Can this access out of bounds memory if `workspace->tiling` shrinks in length during `container_squash`?
Separately, I'm not really sure whether we should be relying on the order containers appear in `workspace->tiling` here (for the skipping). It seems fragile if we don't already do this elsewhere.

I don't think workspace->tiling can shrink in length during the squash. container_squash only modifies the parent by adding containers to it, which is why I keep track of the number added. Containers added to the parent are not themselves eligible to be squashed because the recursion ends when it's done adding them and destroys the container pair. Basically each child has the opportunity to squash one pair of containers in its family, but it stops there.

Regardless, unless I'm sorely mistaken about C (possible), the condition statement is evaluated on each loop, so if length changes the condition value will reflect that and the loop will end rather then set `i >= workspace->length->tiling`. I expect that the length will grow because I am adding containers to it, so I actually need that for correctness. Otherwise the loop will end early.

Actually there is a bug though...  the reap_empty call should decrement change before returning because at that point con and child are certainly empty and will be removed. Atm I guess it skips the immediate sibling of children it successfully squashed.
You're right; I wasn't paying close enough attention.

Separately, I'm not really sure whether we should be relying on the order containers appear in `workspace->tiling` here (for the skipping). It seems fragile if we don't already do this elsewhere.

I don't think workspace->tiling can shrink in length during the squash. container_squash only modifies the parent by adding containers to it, which is why I keep track of the number added. Containers added to the parent are not themselves eligible to be squashed because the recursion ends when it's done adding them and destroys the container pair. Basically each child has the opportunity to squash one pair of containers in its family, but it stops there.

Regardless, unless I'm sorely mistaken about C (possible), the condition statement is evaluated on each loop, so if length changes the condition value will reflect that and the loop will end rather then set `i >= workspace->length->tiling`. I expect that the length will grow because I am adding containers to it, so I actually need that for correctness. Otherwise the loop will end early.

Actually there is a bug though...  the reap_empty call should decrement change before returning because at that point con and child are certainly empty and will be removed. Atm I guess it skips the immediate sibling of children it successfully squashed.
You're right; I wasn't paying close enough attention.
